glossary.definition: A label bound to an object. Assignment binds (or rebinds) a name; it does not copy the object.
What distinguishes one object from another; fixed for the object's life. The is operator compares identities.
An object whose value can change after creation (lists, dictionaries). Numbers, strings and tuples are immutable.
A second name bound to the same object.
Changing an existing object in place, for example with append or item assignment; every name bound to it sees the change.
Pointing a name at a different object, for example y = [9]; other names are unaffected.
A new container holding references to the same items as the original.
A new container holding recursively made copies of the original's items.
A special value, usually None, used as a default meaning 'create a fresh object inside the function'.

routes.title: Core route
routes.description: All three lessons in order, then the capstone.

intro:
This short benchmark course is for someone who already writes Python scripts with loops and functions. In three 25-minute lessons and a capstone you learn to predict what code with aliased, copied and mutated lists prints, debug functions that mutate their arguments by accident, and explain shallow versus deep copies.

Because you chose hands-on practice, each lesson starts with a prediction or a debugging activity before the explanation, and practice asks you to run code in your own Python 3 install. This page never runs Python. Every output shown as 'ran locally' was produced by the course author with python3 3.14.5 and is static text; the interactive trace and evidence widgets display hand-written states.

Sources are the official Python documentation (access date 2026-10-20; the live docs showed Python 3.15 at that date, the behaviour taught here is long-standing Python 3 behaviour).

diagnostic.intro: Four quick questions. They only suggest a pace; nothing is hidden.

questions.prompt: a = [1]; b = a; b.append(2). What is a?
questions.explanation: b and a name the same list.

feedback.0: Assignment b = a does not copy; a is mutated through b.
feedback.2: append adds at the end; it does not replace.

questions.prompt: def f(x): x = x + [0]. Does f(L) change the caller's list L?
questions.explanation: x + [0] builds a new list and rebinds the local x.

feedback.0: Rebinding the local x does not touch the caller's list.

questions.prompt: b = a.copy() where a = [[1],[2]]. Does b[0].append(9) change a?
questions.explanation: copy() is shallow; the inner lists are shared.

feedback.1: copy() only copies the outer list; inner lists are shared.

questions.prompt: def f(v=[]): v.append(1); return v. Two calls f() and f() return?
questions.explanation: The default list is created once.

feedback.0: The default is evaluated once, so it is shared by calls.

capstone.title: Capstone: debug the gradebook
capstone.task:
A teaching assistant's script has three aliasing bugs. Its code is below (it needs no files).

import copy

def make_gradebook(names):
    empty = []
    return {name: empty for name in names}

def record(book, name, score):
    book[name].append(score)

def curve(scores, bonus):
    for i in range(len(scores)):
        scores[i] += bonus
    return scores

def snapshot(book):
    return book.copy()

book = make_gradebook(["ana", "bo"])
record(book, "ana", 70)
print(book)

raw = [60, 70]
curved = curve(raw, 5)
print(raw, curved)

book = {"ana": [70], "bo": [80]}
before = snapshot(book)
record(book, "ana", 90)
print(before)

1. Without running it, predict the three printed lines and say what the author intended instead. 2. Run it in your own Python 3 and compare. 3. Fix each function, naming for each bug whether it is a shared object, a mutating argument, or a shallow copy, and justify the copy depth you chose. 4. Write two sentences explaining to a colleague why the original printed what it did.

descriptors: Predicts fewer than two lines correctly
Predicts two lines, or all with partial reasons
Predicts all three lines and traces each to a shared object
Finds the mutating curve and the shared list but fixes are incomplete
Finds and fixes all bugs without changing intended behaviour, and verifies by running
Distinguishes shallow and deep but justification is generic
Justifies deepcopy for snapshot because the values are mutable lists, and notes costs or when shallow would do

capstone.evaluation: Self-assessed against the rubric. For human feedback, ask a peer or mentor to read your predictions and your explanation before you run the code.
capstone.model: Predicted and actual output (python3 3.14.5, run locally by the course author): {'ana': [70], 'bo': [70]} (both students share one list), [65, 75] [65, 75] (curve mutates the caller's list, so raw is curved too), and {'ana': [70, 90], 'bo': [80]} (a shallow copy shares the score lists). Fixes: {name: [] for name in names}; return [s + bonus for s in scores]; copy.deepcopy(book). After the fixes the course author's run printed {'ana': [70], 'bo': []}, [60, 70] [65, 75], {'ana': [70], 'bo': [80]}. Deepcopy is justified because the values are mutable lists that record() mutates; a dict comprehension copying each list would also work and avoids deep copying unrelated data.
